claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy induces lattice distortions.
A stabilized single-phase solid solution promotes controlled segregation of the noble metal to the nanoparticle surface.
Noble-metal surface segregation forms catalytically active sites.
The resulting active sites enhance catalytic activity and reliability at high temperatures.
A homogeneous precursor containing a low fraction of noble metal can form a high-entropy single-phase solid solution under in-situ processing.
In-situ synthesis is more likely than synthesis from pre-alloyed powders to produce a stabilized single-phase nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles made from pre-alloyed powders are more prone to phase segregation.
High-entropy nanoalloys can be solid-solution nanostructures with lattice distortions and crystalline defects.
Slowed atomic diffusion produces or maintains a noble-metal-enriched surface region.
Lattice distortions and crystalline defects create preferential catalytic surface-reaction sites.
Sluggish atomic diffusion and high-entropy effects suppress deleterious metal or phase segregation.
Sluggish atomic diffusion suppresses nanoparticle coarsening during high-temperature operation.
In-situ-formed nanoparticles will have a more uniform single-phase structure than the pre-alloyed-powder baseline.
In-situ-formed nanoparticles will exhibit greater and more uniform noble-metal surface enrichment than the baseline.
In-situ-formed nanoparticles will have higher catalytic reaction rates or turnover frequencies than the baseline.
In-situ-formed nanoparticles will retain their phase and catalytic performance better during operation at 773–1073 K.
The proposed mechanism applies particularly to 2–20 nm particles operated at 773–1073 K with a noble-metal fraction below 20%.
The quantitative relationships among diffusion rate, surface segregation, and catalytic improvement are not established and may vary with composition and processing.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes noble-metal surface segregation or enrichment to slowed diffusion, while the mechanism also says sluggish diffusion and high entropy suppress segregation. Surface enrichment could coexist with suppression of bulk phase separation, but that distinction and the source of the initial enrichment are not explained.
